stem: A vulnerability scanner reports a critical finding on a server. Investigation confirms the patch was applied two weeks ago and the vulnerability is not present. What is this?

options.text: A false positive
options.why: The tool raised an alarm and there was nothing there. Positive means the tool reported something, false means it was wrong.

options.text: A false negative
options.why: A false negative is silence in the presence of a real problem. Here the tool spoke up.

options.text: A true positive that needs revalidation
options.why: A true positive is a real finding. This was confirmed not to be present.

options.text: A true negative
options.why: A true negative is correct silence. The scanner did not stay silent.

stem: Which outcome is the most dangerous for a detection system, and why?

options.text: A false negative, because a real attack goes unreported
options.why: Nobody is alerted and nobody investigates. The organisation believes it is safe while it is not.

options.text: A false positive, because analysts waste time
options.why: Costly and corrosive through alert fatigue, and still not the outcome that lets an attacker operate undetected.

options.text: A true positive, because it means an attack succeeded
options.why: A true positive means the system worked. Detection is not the same as compromise.

options.text: A true negative, because nothing is logged
options.why: A true negative is correct silence when there is genuinely nothing to report.

stem: A vulnerability on a production system cannot be patched before the next maintenance window six weeks away. Which compensating control reduces exposure most directly in the meantime?

options.text: Segmentation: restrict which hosts can reach the vulnerable service while the patch waits
options.why: Segmentation does not remove the flaw and it removes most of the reachability, which is what turns an exploitable vulnerability into a theoretical one for six weeks.

options.text: Record it as a false positive until the window arrives
options.why: The finding is real. Mislabelling it removes it from the backlog rather than from the estate.

options.text: Rescan weekly to confirm it is still present
options.why: Observation, not mitigation. You will watch it remain exploitable.

options.text: Raise the CVSS environmental score to reflect the risk
options.why: Scoring describes the risk more accurately and changes nothing about exposure.

stem: A report states that a web server is 'probably vulnerable to CVE-2024-1086 based on the version banner', with no evidence the flaw was triggered. Which activity produced this?

options.text: A vulnerability scan
options.why: Scanners infer from versions and responses rather than exploiting. 'Probably, based on the banner' is the signature of inference, and the reason false positives are routine.

options.text: A penetration test
options.why: A penetration test proves exploitability by exploiting. The report would describe what the tester achieved, not what the version implies.

options.text: Static code analysis
options.why: Static analysis reads source or binaries. This finding came from a network-facing banner, with no access to code.

options.text: Package monitoring
options.why: Package monitoring reads a declared dependency manifest. There is no manifest here, only a remote banner.

stem: Leadership asks for evidence of whether an attacker could actually reach the customer database from the internet, chaining whatever weaknesses exist. Which activity answers that question?

options.text: A penetration test
options.why: Only a penetration test chains findings into a path and proves reachability. A list of individual weaknesses does not tell you whether they combine.

options.text: A credentialed vulnerability scan across the estate
options.why: Breadth, not depth. It will enumerate weaknesses thoroughly and tell you nothing about whether they can be strung together.

options.text: A system and process audit against the control framework
options.why: An audit asks whether controls exist and are followed, not whether a determined attacker can get through them anyway.

options.text: Subscribing to a commercial threat feed
options.why: A feed describes what is happening to others. It says nothing about your own path to your own database.

stem: A company publishes a security.txt file and a policy promising not to pursue legal action against researchers who report flaws in good faith. It offers no payment. What has it established?

options.text: A responsible disclosure programme
options.why: The defining feature is a safe, defined channel and an assurance of no reprisal. Payment is what would make it a bounty.

options.text: A bug bounty programme
options.why: A bounty pays per valid finding, usually on a published scale. Without reward it is disclosure, not bounty.

options.text: A penetration testing engagement
options.why: A penetration test is scoped, contracted and paid, with named testers and dates. This is open to anyone who happens to look.

options.text: An information sharing and analysis centre membership
options.why: An ISAC shares threat information among peers in a sector. It is not a channel for outsiders to report flaws in your product.

stem: A security team learns that credentials belonging to its staff are being offered for sale on a criminal forum. Which source most directly provides this?

options.text: Dark web monitoring
options.why: The objectives name this separately because it looks where stolen access is traded, which is often the first sign that a breach already happened.

options.text: Open source intelligence
options.why: OSINT draws on publicly available sources. Criminal marketplaces are not public, which is the whole distinction.

options.text: An information sharing and analysis centre
options.why: An ISAC circulates threat information among sector peers. It would carry the pattern, not your specific credentials.

options.text: A proprietary threat feed of indicators of compromise
options.why: A feed delivers curated indicators such as addresses and hashes, not listings of your own staff accounts for sale.

stem: A tool is pointed at a running staging application, submits crafted input to its forms and endpoints, and reports an injection flaw based on how the application responded. Which technique is this?

options.text: Dynamic analysis
options.why: The application was executing and was probed from outside. Dynamic analysis judges behaviour rather than reading code.

options.text: Static analysis
options.why: Static analysis examines code without running it. Nothing here read the source; everything was inferred from responses.

options.text: Package monitoring
options.why: Package monitoring compares declared dependency versions against known vulnerable ones. It never interacts with a running application.

options.text: A system and process audit
options.why: An audit assesses process and control compliance, not application behaviour under crafted input.

stem: A build pipeline step reads the project's dependency manifest, compares each declared library version against a vulnerability database, and fails the build when a known vulnerable version is present. It never examines the team's own source code. What is this?

options.text: Package monitoring
options.why: It watches the software bill of materials rather than the code. It catches the library you inherited and is blind to the flaw you wrote yourself.

options.text: Static analysis
options.why: Static analysis reads the code itself. This step deliberately does not, which is why both are usually run.

options.text: Dynamic analysis
options.why: Nothing is executed. The check happens against a manifest at build time.

options.text: A vulnerability scan of the build server
options.why: The target is the application's dependencies, not the host the build runs on.

stem: Two findings arrive the same morning. Finding A: CVSS 9.8 on a lab server with no sensitive data, on an isolated segment with no inbound internet path. Finding B: CVSS 7.1 on the internet-facing payment gateway. Which should be remediated first, and why?

options.text: B, because environmental variables and exposure outrank the raw base score
options.why: CVSS base score describes the vulnerability in the abstract. Where the asset sits and what it holds are what turn severity into risk, and the exam tests exactly this inversion.

options.text: A, because 9.8 is critical and 7.1 is only high
options.why: Ranking by the number alone ignores every input the objectives add beside it. A critical flaw on an unreachable host with nothing on it is not your first problem.

options.text: A, because critical findings carry a shorter remediation deadline in policy
options.why: Policy deadlines are usually set against adjusted risk, not raw base score. If yours is not, that is the defect the question is pointing at.

options.text: Neither until both have been confirmed by a penetration test
options.why: Waiting for a test before touching an exposed payment gateway converts a prioritisation problem into a delay.

stem: In a quantitative assessment, a flaw in a document store would destroy roughly 40% of that asset's value if exploited. Which term describes the 40%?

options.text: Exposure factor
options.why: Exposure factor is the proportion of an asset's value lost in a single occurrence. Multiply it by asset value for single loss expectancy.

options.text: Risk tolerance
options.why: Risk tolerance is how much residual risk the organisation is willing to carry. It is a decision, not a measurement of loss.

options.text: The CVSS environmental score
options.why: The environmental metric adjusts CVSS for your deployment. It is a severity rating, not a fraction of asset value.

options.text: Annualised rate of occurrence
options.why: That is how often you expect it per year, not how much each occurrence costs.

stem: A vulnerability cannot be patched because the vendor has ended support for the application, which is required for production. The organisation documents the decision, assigns an owner, applies network segmentation, and sets a review date six months out. What has been recorded?

options.text: An exception with a compensating control, accepted within the organisation's risk tolerance
options.why: A legitimate exception has an owner, a justification, a compensating control and an expiry. All four are present, which is what separates this from ignoring the finding.

options.text: A false positive, since the vulnerability cannot be remediated
options.why: A false positive is a finding that was never real. This one is real, acknowledged, and deliberately carried.

options.text: Remediation, because segmentation removes the vulnerability
options.why: Segmentation reduces reachability. The vulnerable code is still present and would still execute if reached.

options.text: An exemption, which unlike an exception does not expire
options.why: The review date is the tell. An open-ended acceptance with no expiry is precisely what turns a backlog permanent.

stem: After a patch is applied, the next scan no longer reports the finding. An engineer argues this is not sufficient evidence the vulnerability is gone. What is the strongest basis for that argument?

options.text: A rescan only shows the scanner no longer detects it, which a firewall rule or a changed banner can also produce
options.why: Rescanning and verification answer different questions. Suppressing detection is not the same as removing the condition, and this is the distinction the objectives draw.

options.text: Scanners always produce false negatives after patching
options.why: Too strong. The point is that a quiet scanner is weak evidence, not that it is always wrong.

options.text: The patch must be approved through change management before it counts
options.why: Process compliance matters but is a separate question from whether the weakness is technically gone.

options.text: Only a penetration test can confirm remediation
options.why: Verification can be a targeted check of the specific condition. Commissioning a full test for every patch is neither necessary nor affordable.

stem: A vulnerability management programme produces monthly figures on open findings by severity, mean time to remediate, and findings past their due date. What is the primary purpose of this activity within the programme?

options.text: Reporting: giving risk owners the trend and the exceptions they must decide on
options.why: Reporting closes the loop upward. Counts alone are vanity; what makes it reporting is that it puts decisions in front of the people who own the risk.

options.text: Auditing the vulnerability management process
options.why: An audit is an independent assessment of whether the process is followed. Producing your own metrics is not an audit of yourself.

options.text: Verification that remediations were effective
options.why: Verification is a per-finding technical check, not an aggregate monthly figure.

options.text: Prioritising which findings to remediate next
options.why: Prioritisation uses severity, exposure and environment per finding. Trend metrics inform the programme rather than ranking individual work.

stem: CVE-2021-44228 and CVSS 10.0 appear in the same advisory. What is the relationship between the two identifiers?

options.text: The CVE names the specific vulnerability; the CVSS score rates how severe it is
options.why: CVE is an identifier from a catalogue so everyone means the same flaw. CVSS is a scoring system producing a number from metrics. One names, the other rates.

options.text: The CVE is the severity rating and the CVSS is the catalogue entry
options.why: Reversed. CVE carries no severity at all, which is precisely why CVSS exists alongside it.

options.text: Both are severity scores, maintained by different bodies
options.why: CVE is an identifier and nothing more. It does not rank anything.

options.text: The CVE applies to software and the CVSS applies to hardware
options.why: Neither is limited by target type. The split between them is naming versus scoring.

stem: Beyond the CVSS base score, which TWO inputs does the SY0-701 blueprint expect to shape how a vulnerability is prioritised? (Choose two.)

options.text: Environmental variables, such as whether the asset is internet-facing or segmented
options.why: Where the asset sits changes reachability, and reachability is most of real risk.

options.text: Industry and organisational impact, such as regulated data or safety-critical function
options.why: The same flaw carries a different consequence in healthcare, payments or a utility, which is why the blueprint names it separately.

options.text: The number of findings the team closed last month
options.why: Throughput is a programme metric. It says nothing about which finding matters most.

options.text: Whether the finding came from a scan or a penetration test
options.why: The source affects confidence in the finding, not its intrinsic priority once confirmed.

options.text: The alphabetical order of the affected hostnames
options.why: Included as a reminder that an arbitrary ordering is still an ordering, and it is the one a backlog defaults to without deliberate prioritisation.

stem: A regional hospital group wants early warning of attack campaigns specifically targeting healthcare providers, shared by other hospitals. Which source fits best?

options.text: An information sharing and analysis centre for the health sector
options.why: ISACs exist to circulate sector-specific threat information among peers, which is the only source here where the other members share the reporter's threat profile.

options.text: A proprietary commercial threat feed
options.why: Useful and timely, but curated by a vendor for a broad customer base rather than by peers facing the same sector-specific adversaries.

options.text: Open source intelligence gathered from public reporting
options.why: Free and broad, but by the time a campaign is publicly reported the early warning has usually passed.

options.text: Dark web monitoring
options.why: That surfaces data and access already being traded, which is late-stage rather than early warning of a campaign.
